title: Adaptive Progress Checkpointing Optimized for Interruption Risk and Verified Recovery
target_platform: Multi-agent coordination harness; manage_coordination.py; relay.py; evaluating-agent-work telemetry (ceiling 1M tokens, 12 execution-hours)
hypothesis: A checkpoint policy using measured interruption risk, progress value, and checkpoint cost will: (a) produce >= 20% more verified completed subgoals per fixed resource budget than the best fixed-interval policy on development data; (b) lose <= 5% of acknowledged progress; (c) keep checkpoint overhead <= 10% of inference tokens; and (d) lose no more than 3% throughput in interruption-free controls.
falsification_criteria: Fail if any threshold is missed, or if the adaptive policy uses advance knowledge of the held-out interruption schedule.
experiment: Run 30 multi-stage tasks under frozen interruption schedules (context reset, worker termination, simulated quota denial, vendor handoff). Compare fixed-step checkpoints, fixed-time checkpoints, end-only persistence, and the adaptive policy. Score independently verified subgoals, not self-reported completion.

model_routing.frontier_escalation_condition: Frontier models are limited to participating in multi-vendor handoff tests under the 1M token ceiling.

evidence.details: Frozen v2 candidate (cold-start repair with pre-registered prior), all 630 planned trials complete (simulation 1,620 trials; real-agent arm with local Qwen: 30 tasks x 7 policies x development/held-out/control). Simulation: gain -14.9% dev / -11.6% held-out (needs >=20%), acknowledged loss 47.7% / 46.2% (needs <=5%), control throughput loss 3.5998% (needs <=3%). Real arm: gain -78.0% dev / -71.7% held-out, loss 93.2% / 90.9%, checkpoint overhead 7.6-8.0% (pass), control loss 0.0% frozen measure and 1.09% by request service time (pass by construction: adaptive behaved as end-only, 0 early requests in 90 trials). Independent reviews (Claude reviewer of Codex work): simulation accepted; real arm changes-requested then fixed (adaptive == end-only by arithmetic; budget infeasible: even the best fixed policy loses 57-58%; 1,113/1,282 wrong calls were identical deterministic repeats; ~46% of budget unused; v2 prior chosen post hoc after v1 held-out). Scope: this frozen design and candidate, not adaptive checkpointing in general; handoff and quota denial simulated; real arm tested a sequential request driver, not a live long-context agent. Contention: 58% of summed wall time was lock wait; metrics are token-based; control claim re-checked on service time; one interrupted trial preserved and rerun, reproduced exactly.

lessons_learned: A policy whose trigger cannot fire inside the trial budget degenerates to the baseline; check feasibility before a real-agent run.
Interrupted trials: preserve the partial snapshot, rerun deterministically, exclude by explicit response id, assert reproduction.
A shared model lock held by the orchestrator can stall a worker that misreads the wait as a timeout.
